memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "This is to be a lasting ordinance for you: On the tenth day of the seventh month you must deny yourselves and not do any work — whether native-born or a foreigner residing among you — because on this day atonement will be made for you, to cleanse you. Then, before the LORD, you will be clean from all your sins." - Lev 16:29-30 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Two commands, and they sit together strangely: deny yourselves, and do no work.

Denying yourself sounds active. Doing no work sounds passive. But both point the same direction — away from self-reliance. On the day their sins were dealt with, Israel was forbidden from doing anything at all. They fasted. They rested. They watched.

Because atonement was not their work. It was being done for them.

That is the hardest lesson for religious people to learn. We would far rather contribute something. We want a role in our own salvation, some effort that makes us feel we earned a portion of it. God says: sit down. It is for you that atonement is being made.

For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith — and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God — not by works, so that no one can boast (Eph 2:8-9).

And notice who is included: whether native-born or a foreigner residing among you. Even then, God's cleansing was not limited to those born into Israel. The door was open wider than people expected.

You will be clean from all your sins. All. Not most.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you still try to contribute something to your own salvation?
2. What would it mean to genuinely rest in Christ's finished work?
3. How does the word "all" speak to something you are still carrying?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, teach me to stop working for what You have already accomplished. Thank You that atonement was made for me, and that in Christ I am clean from all my sins. Amen.
